- list 2 of 4Macron lines up more Gulf diesel as France battles soaring fuel prices
- list 3 of 4‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal
- list 4 of 4UK approves development of Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
Russia lifted its ban on diesel exports on October 9, which Moscow originally put in place to tackle the country’s shortages as Ukrainian-led drone strikes hindered production capacity.
The shipment comes despite setbacks for Russia’s diesel output. Earlier this month, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said that drone strikes knocked out at least half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, forcing cuts at Russia’s top diesel-producing refineries.
“Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States’ needs, to the extent of our capabilities,” the RIA Novosti news agency quoted Novak as saying.
That was echoed by US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has been meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks in St Petersburg.
“We are preparing deliveries of several vessels, the tankers, right now. They will go one after another. The financial component should be provided,” he said, adding that Russia would also be able to supply fertilisers in “large quantities” to the US market.
US President Donald Trump had previously said that Moscow would export 300,000 tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.
US consumers have continued to face high prices at the petrol station, particularly for diesel fuel, a pressing point as the country heads into midterm elections in less than two weeks. The average price for a gallon of diesel is $6.31 ($1.70 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). While prices remain well over the $6 mark, they are on the downturn. The average price a month ago was $6.51.

articles.title: Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: The pledge, which Trump says will go through tax-friendly 'Trump accounts', comes two weeks before the US midterms.
articles.full_text:
Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
The pledge, which Trump says will go through accounts with his name, comes two weeks before the US midterms.
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.
“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.
About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data.
At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn.
President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year.
The pledge comes two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.
Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July.
Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how.
So how might the giveaway work, and who stands to gain?
Here’s what you need to know:
How much is a SpaceX share worth, and how much is Musk giving away?
SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share.
That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing.
The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m.
Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August.
Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company.
Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation.
It would be the largest single gift linked to Trump accounts so far.
How would the shares reach children?
Musk has not said.
Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”.
Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status.
Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds.
Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner.
Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Who gains?
The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift.
He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”.
The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation.
The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”.
Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money.
Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported.
As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn.
It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May.
Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”.
For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet.
For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts.
“It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.”
Why is the timing important?
The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election.
Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.
Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.
Is this legal, and why is it controversial?
Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns.
“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”
But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.
Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate.
Has anyone done this before?
Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”.
Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.
He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.
Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

articles.title: Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard after four years in prison
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Hubbard was jailed after being accused of fighting alongside Ukrainian forces against Russia.
articles.full_text:
Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard after four years in prison
Hubbard was jailed after Russia said he fought alongside Ukrainian forces against Russia.
American Stephen Hubbard has been freed from a Russian prison and is on his way home after United States President Donald Trump said his administration had secured his release.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, adding that the US was not required to give anything in return for the release of the 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Russia frees US basketball star Brittney Griner in prisoner swap
- list 2 of 3Griner’s release raises fresh concerns about fate of Paul Whelan
- list 3 of 3Russia frees ex-US Marine Robert Gilman from detention
The deal came during a visit to Russia by a top US envoy, and just days after Trump took a series of actions seen as beneficial to Moscow.
Hubbard, whose family says had been living in Ukraine since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, was tried and convicted in a closed-door trial, with Russian prosecutors saying he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military and had fought alongside its forces before being captured. He was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2024.
The US had declared Hubbard a wrongfully detained American.
Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is in Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin on the Ukraine war, told him that “our whole nation sends their thanks” and that Putin was a “humanitarian” for allowing Hubbard to walk free. Witkoff briefly met with Hubbard in St. Petersburg after his release, telling him, “from today is a new life for you”.
The release came at a dynamic moment in relations between the US, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship under strain at the same time that the Trump administration has pursued policies which Ukraine says have rewarded Putin.
Those include Trump’s decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that the US Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.
Named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in an effort to curb high gas prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

articles.title: US congressional candidate Brad Lander freed after West Bank detention
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Lander says dozens remain in Israeli custody after being detained while helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives.
articles.full_text:
US congressional candidate Brad Lander freed after West Bank detention
Lander says dozens remain in Israeli custody after being detained while helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives.
United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander says he has been released from Israeli military custody with a warning after being detained alongside dozens of volunteers helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.
But several dozen others, including rabbis and international volunteers, remain in detention, according to Lander, who called for them to be released immediately.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3How Israel’s 2026 election works
- list 2 of 3Far from fringe: How Israel’s mainstream parties vote with the far right
- list 3 of 3From one house to villages: Israeli settlers have Palestinians surrounded
“I’ve been released from IDF custody with a ‘warning,’ apparently because of my public profile,” Lander wrote on X. “I told them I wasn’t even a congressmember yet, just a nominee.”
Lander, a Jewish American and former New York City comptroller, was among approximately 80 volunteers detained by Israeli soldiers and police near the village of Nahalin, outside Bethlehem, according to the Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights.
The group included American, Israeli, Palestinian, British and Canadian volunteers.
Beck Strober, a representative of the Protect the Harvest Coalition, which helped organize the olive harvest, told Al Jazeera that the group had been peacefully picking olives at the invitation of a Palestinian family for several hours when the Israeli army arrived.
“It was a nice, peaceful day,” he said. “There was no conflict. There was no settler violence. There was no violence of any kind.”
According to Strober, after a while, soldiers began checking the volunteers’ IDs, and soon after, issued an order declaring the area a closed military zone. They then detained the group, first in the field and later at a police station.
“To this moment, everyone’s still detained except for Brad Lander,” said Strober. “They very clearly told him that they allowed him to be released because he’s likely to be in Congress very soon.”
Anton Goodman, acting director for Rabbis for Human Rights, told Reuters that volunteers who were neither Israeli nor Palestinian citizens were expected to be transferred to an Israeli military base.
In a video posted on X from one of the buses, Lander said Israeli forces had detained the group after apparently being called to the area by settlement security personnel.
“We’ve been detained by the Israeli military for harvesting olives,” he said. “And let’s be clear, occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives is not a crime under any law.”
It’s not clear why the area was declared a closed military zone. Rabbis for Human Rights said they had no way of knowing about the order and had offered to leave voluntarily when they were told.
Lander said the volunteers had been taken away for processing but had not been told whether they were under arrest.
Lander, a vocal critic of Israel’s war on Gaza, is a former New York City mayoral candidate and an ally of Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He’s now running as the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th congressional district in the November 3 midterm elections.
Writing on X after his release, Lander said Palestinians face worse consequences every day.
“These detentions by the IDF are one more attempt to undermine Palestinians’ right to harvest their olive groves, travel on their roads, and live in their homes,” he wrote. “Yet one more element of escalating, and very clearly state-sponsored, ethnic cleansing.
Neither the Israeli government nor the US Embassy in Jerusalem immediately responded to a request for comment.
The volunteers had travelled to the West Bank to support Palestinian farmers during the annual olive harvest, amid a surge in settler violence, including several attacks in recent days targeting Palestinians and international observers.
Stober said Wednesday was the first time the Palestinian family had been able to access its own land since October 7, 2023 because violence in the area had made it too dangerous to return.
“The fact that Brad was thee, of course, made the situation more newsworthy, but we’ve been seeing this happen in the West Bank for years.”
On Friday, an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was beaten by Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest. The following day, European diplomats and a French mayor were attacked by settlers during another harvest. Palestinians were also attacked in both incidents.
Israeli police said on Tuesday they had arrested 10 people in connection with the attacks.

articles.title: Got milk? US Army refines its pasteurization power
articles.snippet: Thirteen U.S. Army Veterinary Corps officers milked a trip to Denmark last month, completing Europe Dairy Pasteurization Audit Training.
articles.full_text:
Thirteen U.S. Army Veterinary Corps officers milked a trip to Denmark last month, completing Europe Dairy Pasteurization Audit Training in the seaport city of Kolding.
The service said the course — which included on-site field evaluations at eight Danish dairy facilities currently approved for U.S. military procurement — aimed to ensure military members and their families overseas receive dairy that meets or exceeds U.S. standards.
In the U.S., commercial milk must be processed according to the Food and Drug Administration’s Pasteurized Milk Ordinance. Because commercial pasteurization methods are “udderly” different across the world, the course gives officers the skills to evaluate pasteurization technology in different regions, the Army said in a Monday release. The course has been taught and revised since 2004.
Military auditors from around the world, including Public Health Command Pacific, Area Support Group Kuwait and Public Multinational Force and Observers Egypt, trained to improve their pasteurization skills. Public Health Command Europe is unique, the service said, because it offers military inspectors the chance to see more than 65 pasteurizer setups.
During the course, led by Chief Warrant Officer 4 Clayton Davenport, the command food safety officer for Public Health Command Europe, the Army said officers gained realistic experience assessing equipment in operation.
“The primary training objective was to provide progressive and sequential auditor development training in pasteurizer operations that enhances understanding of the public health controls of various pasteurizers,” Davenport said in the release. “Maintaining specialized auditing capabilities remains essential to force health protection, particularly amid budgetary pressures.”
Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

articles.title: German military raises sabotage threat level amid warning of Russian attacks: report
articles.snippet: German forces themselves could face attacks at home, according to a classified internal analysis reported by public broadcaster WDR and newspaper SZ.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — Germany’s military, the Bundeswehr, has raised its assessment of the Russian sabotage threat to its second-highest level, warning that German forces themselves could face attacks at home, according to a classified internal analysis reported by public broadcaster WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung on Oct. 21.
The report’s findings point to a potentially broader threat than German military security specialists had previously anticipated. Their concerns had centered on installations training Ukrainian troops, alongside naval bases and shipyards. The new assessment says authorities can no longer geographically confine specific sites deemed vulnerable, warning instead of an all-around deterioration in the security situation, with concrete actions possible in the near term.
The reassessment follows the discovery of an apparently crashed drone near Wunstorf air base in northern Germany in September. Investigators found a can containing explosives a few meters away, according to the report. They suspect the aircraft may have targeted military planes rather than civilian cargo aircraft.
WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that investigators believe the Wunstorf drone had lain near the base for about two years, citing technical analysis by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office. Its construction resembled an explosives-equipped drone used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, the outlets reported, though it would have significantly predated the Leipzig incident.
The military analysis draws a distinction between the two incidents: While Leipzig presented an indirect threat to German forces, targeting Ukrainian aircraft instead, Wunstorf likely involved the Bundeswehr itself as the target. The assessment describes Russia as almost certainly possessing the capability, and very likely an increased motivation, to act against German forces and facilities, as well as Ukrainian partners in Germany.
It also concludes that Russia’s use of drones as weapons crossed a previously anticipated “red line” involving an intention to cause physical damage or potentially lethal effects.
The German government has publicly attributed the Leipzig drone attack to Russia following a month-long investigation.
The analysis links the suspected campaign to efforts to weaken political and public support for Ukraine in Germany. At the operational level, it assesses that Moscow seeks to disrupt equipment deliveries and training, undermining Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
An Operational Command spokesperson told WDR that the Bundeswehr currently considers the sabotage risk “substantial” because of the increased threat. This places it at the second-highest level of the military’s risk assessment scale, SZ reported.
The military is strengthening protective measures at its installations to safeguard personnel and facilities, the spokesperson said.
The warning follows suspicious drone flights over sites associated with Germany’s Arrow 3 missile-defense system and Patriot maintenance facilities. German security authorities suspect Russian involvement in those and other surveillance incidents, WDR reported.
Russia has consistently denied involvement in sabotage and hybrid attacks, and has blamed Germany for staging incidents to whip up anti-Russian sentiment. Moscow’s ambassador to Berlin previously dismissed Germany’s allegations over Leipzig as “absurd” and described the incident as a “provocation.”
Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

articles.title: Timing to roll out US Army’s NGC2 depends on funds, commander says
articles.snippet: The head of the Army formation responsible for fielding the Next Generation Command and Control system said the timeline depends on resources available.
articles.full_text:
The head of the U.S. Army formation leading the charge for fielding the service’s next-gen command-and-control system said Oct. 13 that the timeline of implementing the tech hinged on factors above his pay grade.
Commander of I Corps Lt. Gen. Matt McFarlane told reporters at a media roundtable in Washington that the desire to see the platform deployed across the formation by the end of fiscal 2027 was dependent on what the service was able to provide.
“Scaling and speed up is based on resources available,” said McFarlane. “That’s not in my job jar.”
The Army’s NGC2 platform will permit technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications from across the force to co-exist on the same network, streamlining decision-making during combat environments.
As the service expands the new platform across the I Corps, which oversees troops across the Indo-Pacific, the Army will get a close-up look at how the system allows military personnel and machines to communicate with each other over vast geographical distances and in communication-contested environments.
Among its many responsibilities, the I Corps works with Security Assistance Group-Ukraine, a U.S.-led joint military command headquartered in Germany that provides weapons and training support to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
I Corps uses SAG-U to digest lessons learned from the unique military dynamics of the war in Ukraine and determine how to apply them to other potential conflicts worldwide.
The Army recently awarded defense tech company Anduril Industries a contract worth up to $1.8 billion to continue developing NGC2’s common data baseline, or software foundation.
Anduril, along with Palantir, Raft and Striveworks, has been refining the technology to help the service move NGC2 from the experimental phase to fielding.
The resources McFarlane referred to include funds, which are currently up in the air as the Senate still works to pass the National Defense Authorization Act.
With Congress currently in recess, the timeline for approval of those funds is murky.
The Army’s proposed budget for fiscal 2027 includes a $904 million request for the research, development and scaling of NGC2.
Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.

articles.title: US Marine Corps makes Maven available service-wide
articles.snippet: The service made the AI-enabled battlefield management system available to all commands and organizations within the service.
articles.full_text:
The Marine Corps announced a new licensing agreement that allows all commands and organizations across the service, including the reserves, to access the Maven Smart System, or MSS, through any applicable network.
“This enterprise licensing provides all assigned and attached personnel at any echelon within the specified commands the ability to gain MSS accounts within those domains they have authorized access,” the service said in last week’s announcement.
Maven is an AI-enabled software platform owned by the government but developed by the company Palantir. The system aggregates and analyzes data from several feeds like intelligence reports, drone video, satellite imagery, maps and more in support of real-time decision-making by commanders and analysts across services and allies.
For example, Defense Department officials say they used Maven to identify and bomb more than 2,000 distinct targets in Iran within the first 96 hours of Operation Epic Fury. Officials add that the system is used to process about 6 million pages of text per day for intelligence and operational workflows.
Ahead of a Maven training summit in August, the Marine Corps also explained that its demand for Maven has grown, noting that some 5,500 Marines used the system in the month prior. Additionally, the Marines replaced its manual process for filing Situational Reports with a Maven application.
Before the Oct. 1 agreement, the service’s license only allowed specific commands and organizations to use the AI-enabled battle management system and only through a Secret Internet Protocol Router Network, or SIPRNet. In that August 2025 rollout, the service provided dozens of units with access and training to the system.
The Marine Corps is encouraging commands to designate an MSS implementation lead for their respective organization. The service said that training materials are available on the secure website Intelink. It added that further guidance such as an MSS Implementation Plan will be published separately.
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

articles.title: Europe weighs giving utilities, infrastructure companies more powers to bring down drones
articles.snippet: Offials are worried that drone attacks could knock out power to millions of people — as has happened frequently in Ukraine after Russian strikes.
articles.full_text:
At a former flight-test base south of Paris, drones swoop over fields and woodland as teams on the ground test systems designed to stop them — a response to a growing wave of drone incursions and “hybrid attacks” since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
The potential clients for technology such as electronic jammers and interceptor drones tested at the Brétigny-sur-Orge site are no longer just governments, police and armies.
Private firms and state entities across Europe that operate critical infrastructure want to strengthen their defenses, with some utilities asking for authorization to shoot drones down themselves. From Paris to Berlin, governments are taking note.
They are worried that hybrid warfare or a drone attack could knock out power to millions of people — as has happened frequently in Ukraine after Russian strikes.
RELATED
“It is a theoretical, and increasingly a practical, possibility that there could be heating outages this winter due to hybrid attacks,” Kristian Ruby, secretary general of European energy body Eurelectric, told Reuters.
Some European governments are responding by starting to give firms powers traditionally confined to the military. Interviews by Reuters with over 30 company executives, officials and drone experts meanwhile show the technology to detect and bring down drones is maturing faster than the rules on who may use it.
Approaches vary widely across Europe and legal uncertainties remain, including over who has the right to order a response to a drone threat. Bringing down a drone could cause injury or death to people on the ground or damage property, raising questions for companies about liability and accountability.
“Defenseless”
France is among countries that have led the way. Its parliament passed a law in August allowing approved operators of critical infrastructure and contractors to detect, jam and shoot down drones near designated facilities.
The law passed by the French parliament in August responded to a wave of drone incursions over critical and military sites, including flights over the Ile Longue nuclear submarine base near Brest in northwestern France in December 2025.
France wants a newly expanded list of sensitive sites deemed of vital importance equipped by 2027, a senior French official involved in the plans told Reuters, asking not to be named because details of the plan are not yet public.
“We were defenseless in the face of the (drone) threat,” the official said, adding that concerns had been growing over the last decade as unmanned aerial vehicles became more accessible and more common.
The French government wants to give operators of critical infrastructure such as state-owned utility company EDF and state-owned railway company SNCF a catalogue of approved systems ranging from electronic jammers to interceptor drones, depending on different environments and situations.
Confirming important elements of the plan outlined by the French official, Systematic Paris-Region, which runs the government testing program at Brétigny-sur-Orge, said evaluations launched this summer had so far catalogued three systems integrators — which combine different computer systems into a unified whole — and 17 counter-drone systems.
It said assessments were continuing and work was underway to accelerate procurement from among those solutions.
France’s defense ministry said the law passed in August would help strengthen capabilities to counter the threat, though it said it could speak only for the critical infrastructure under its authority. EDF and SNCF declined comment.
Who can bring down a drone?
The discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle airport in August underlined how far the risks have spread.
Germany blamed Russia for the incident. Moscow denied it was behind it, and has repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe, many of which have been in countries that support Kyiv in Russia’s war in Ukraine.
But concerns are growing that national authorities cannot respond fast enough to protect widely dispersed infrastructure against such attacks, and that the damage caused by relatively cheap drones could bring hefty repair costs.
In Germany, where counter-drone operations remain a policing function, the interior ministry told Reuters it was reviewing how critical infrastructure operators and third parties could be legally involved in active counter-drone measures.
In September, Austria announced plans to give similar powers to critical infrastructure operators, including large energy firms. Defense Minister Klaudia Tanner told a press conference that the state could not protect every site on its own.
Poland has gone further. Operators told Reuters they have deployed counter-drone systems and trained with military and police units. Drone-restricted zones have been established around critical energy infrastructure, and designated security units working for operators have been authorized to destroy, disable or take control of drones entering them.
But two sources at energy transmission companies on NATO’s eastern flank told Reuters that effective intervention still requires more assurances, and perhaps a judicial precedent, on who bears responsibility for collateral damage.
Without that certainty, they said, operators of critical infrastructure could remain reluctant to neutralize drones because bringing one down could itself cause injury or costly damage.
Built for recovery
Having powers to bring down drones would be a change of approach for companies across Europe.
Executives, officials and energy analysts told Reuters that utilities have spent years hardening networks and preparing to restore disrupted services, rather than preventing attacks.
Leonhard Birnbaum, chief executive of German energy firm E.ON, said in September that operators must assume some attacks will succeed, rather than plan on stopping all of them. The company operates about 2,720 substations across Germany, he said.
Lithuania is building a fortified substation near its border with Russia as part of plans by the Baltic states and Poland to improve their defenses that include constructing bunkers, installing anti-drone nets and building up stocks of hard-to-replace equipment for critical parts of the energy grid.
Poland’s state-owned transmission operator PSE patrols parts of its about 16,500-km (10,250-mile) high-voltage network by helicopter and is preparing more powerful aircraft to help protect an undersea power link to Sweden.
Yet relatively inexpensive drones are challenging such defenses. Essential equipment such as large transformers can take years to replace, while even a successful repair can leave infrastructure out of service for months.
Not all utility operators are seeking a bigger role in defending themselves.
Asta Sihvonen-Punkka, chief executive of Finland’s national power grid operator Fingrid, told Reuters that responsibility for countering threats around critical infrastructure should remain with Finnish authorities and armed forces.
Any move to give such powers to utility operators would be “a very, very big change” requiring careful legal consideration, she said.
Jari Stenius, head of security of Finnish utility Fortum, said he was content for energy companies to focus on producing energy while police and military authorities handled security threats.
Technology ready, rules are not
Security officials and counter-drone technology firms say systems are becoming increasingly automated because operators cannot station specialist teams at every site.
Modern counter-drone systems combine sensors, command-and-control software and countermeasures into a single chain designed to identify, classify and respond to threats within seconds.
Several companies told Reuters that uncertainty over who can authorize a response has slowed investment in the latter stages of that process. France is therefore trying to automate the process as much as possible, said the senior French official involved in France’s plans.
The official said security workers at utilities should eventually be able to detect a threat and launch an automated response at the press of a button, because having operators trained to use military-grade solutions at every location was unrealistic.
German defense company Rheinmetall told Reuters the biggest hurdle for civilian operators was often the delay between detecting a drone and deciding whether to deploy a countermeasure, as legal responsibilities remain fragmented.
Rheinmetall said interest from private infrastructure operators in counter-drone systems was rising sharply.
The company said it was conducting workshops, site surveys and infrastructure assessments for operators and was preparing for what it described as a “very fast-growing” market segment.
(Reporting by Maria Rugamer and Leo Marchandon in Gdansk, Florence Loeve in Paris and Marek Strzelecki in Warsaw.)

articles.title: Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer tapped as Barracks Task Force senior advisor
articles.snippet: Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer was selected as Secretary Hegseth's senior advisor and will visit military installations across the country.
articles.full_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appointed Medal of Honor recipient and U.S. Marine Corps reservist Dakota Meyer to the Pentagon’s Barracks Task Force.
Meyer will now serve as Hegseth’s senior advisor to the task force, which is tasked with addressing the military’s “unacceptable” living conditions, the defense secretary announced Monday in a video on social media.
“Our warfighters should be focused on training, readiness and defending this great nation,” Meyer said during the video. “They shouldn’t have to fight for basic living conditions when they come home at night.”
As senior advisor, Meyer will travel to installations across the country, looking at their barracks, meeting with service members and identifying how to curtail any issues blocking the resolutions.
The first group of installations Meyer is expected to visit are all located in California, with Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed by Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms on Thursday and Marine Corps Air Station Miramar on Friday.
If sticking to schedule, Meyer will have visited 21 bases across the country, with most along the East Coast, by the end of December, according to a map displayed during the social media video.
“I want you to ask this question for the next couple of months: Where’s Dakota?” Hegseth posed during the video. “Could he be coming to my base, to my installation, to my camp, my fort? Because he might be.”
“He’ll be traversing the country on behalf of the Barracks Task Force, on behalf of me personally inspecting, holding town halls, getting real input, and then providing real solutions,” Hegseth continued. “Be on the lookout for him.”
Hegseth first formed the task force in October 2025 to be led by the assistant secretary of defense for energy, installations and environment. The group is meant to identify investment opportunities and create department-wide policies for barracks standards.
The One Bill Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed into law in July 2025, gave the Defense Department $1.2 billion for barracks improvement, with $230 million allotted for the Marine Corps Barracks 2030 initiative and $425 million for enlisted boot camp barracks and other related facilities, as well as $1 billion for Army, Navy, Air Force and Space Force restoration and modernization of military housing.
A Government Accountability Office report from August found that the Defense Department does not request enough funding to meet its installation maintenance and improvement needs, resulting in an estimated $285 billion of maintenance backlogs in fiscal 2025.
Previous GAO reports found that some barracks were “chronically neglected,” resulting in poor conditions that impacted enlisted service members’ quality of life. Thousands of service members lived in subpar barracks, with some having potentially serious health and safety risks, according to a 2023 report.
Recently, the Barracks Task Force funded various projects at installations across the nation, including modernized housing at Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield, Georgia, and a housing installation at Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton, Washington.
“From this point forward, there’s no confusion about who’s accountable,” Meyer posted on social media. “If we don’t get this fixed, there’s only one person to blame. Me.”
Former President Barack Obama awarded Meyer his Medal of Honor in 2011 for his service during the Battle of Ganjgal in Afghanistan in 2009 when he repeatedly entered an enemy ambush zone to rescue wounded comrades and recover the bodies of fallen service members. His actions were credited with saving 13 Americans and 23 Afghan personnel.
Meyer left the Marine Corps in 2010 and reenlisted in the reserves in April 2025, with his oath of enlistment administered at the Pentagon by Hegseth.
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: US Army support for Golden Dome missile shield takes shape
articles.snippet: A U.S. Army air defense unit has been "earmarked" for support of the Golden Dome for America project, an Army official confirmed.
articles.full_text:
As the U.S. Army’s support to the joint force space mission takes shape with its newly populated Space Operations Branch, the service is also poised to support what’s expected to be a critical year for testing and development of the Golden Dome for America (GDA) missile shield project.
Speaking with reporters at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting last week, Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, commanding general of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, confirmed that an Army air defense unit had been “earmarked” for GDA support.
The unit, which he declined to identify, is “a well-trained organization that we know can meet the demands of Golden Dome for America when the systems are fielded,” Rafferty said.
With the current air defense systems across the joint force grouped in aggregated packages, including a sensor, an interceptor and a command-and-control package, Rafferty said he understood GDA as a way to do some disaggregation and bring together command-and-control systems into a group that can work together across the United States.
“So now, as you array sensors and interceptors and C2 platforms across the country, you can use any sensor, best shooter, right C2, in that disaggregated way,” he said. “So we believe that right now … we have the most experienced air defense and combat-seasoned air defense formations in the world [and] we have the right people with the right experience to manage the system when they get here, with some training.”
Joint Task Force Gold, a 100-person unit established in January under U.S. Northern Command and led by Army officers, is also leaning into preparation for Golden Dome with planning drills and stakeholder gatherings, said Col. Kevin “Stoney” Stonerook, deputy commander of the task force.
“We are helping put together the team of teams, all the different stakeholder communities, be that vendors and other government agencies, to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA,” Stonerook said. “We definitely know that we are involved in putting together some of the sites as we look at building out GDA across the country and other areas, and trying to integrate all those capabilities across the multiple layers of GDA, but there’s a lot we still have to figure out.”
The task force, he said, had hosted a series of planning “sprints” beginning in February, working with about 300 members of the “GDA stakeholder community” on-site in Colorado Springs to hash out a concept of operations for the project and to identify unanswered questions.
The next planning sprint, Stonerook said, was set for the end of October.
“We’re continuing to find out more and help focus the efforts of not just the JTF-Gold 100-plus personnel, but all the rest of the stakeholder communities to really focus on those questions needing to be answered for … operationalization,” he said.
Pentagon officials have said they’re looking to field an early version of GDA by the end of next year — to meet a goal of having an operational shield by the end of President Donald Trump’s second term, with a more fully realized version of the system to be built out by 2035.
But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have expressed frustration with slow progress and inconsistent communication from the White House over the way forward with the ambitious and expensive project.
The Pentagon requested $17.5 billion for Golden Dome in fiscal 2027 through a $350 billion reconciliation package, and just about $400 million for the project in research and development funds, within the base budget request. As Air and Space Forces Magazine reported in September, dispute over passage of the reconciliation bill could leave the bulk of funding in jeopardy.
At the panel with reporters, Rafferty maintained the Army was all in on supporting development of the shield system.
“I really try to draw no distinction between [Army Space and Missile Defense Command] and JTF-Gold,” he said. “It’s going to take all of us to help enable the defense of the homeland through Golden Dome for America, and it is SMDC’s No. 1 priority to protect the homeland. So we’re all in to help to deliver that.”

articles.title: US Air Force F-22 pilot controls unmanned FQ-44 in flight
articles.snippet: The fighter jet’s pilot served as an airborne “quarterback” and gave high-level directives to an Anduril-made Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
articles.full_text:
An F-22 Raptor controlled a YFQ-44A Collaborative Combat Aircraft, advancing the U.S. Air Force’s efforts to produce the service’s “loyal wingmen.”
The F-22 completed airborne tactical command and in-flight control of a YFQ-44A Fury earlier this month, the Air Force announced.
The fighter jet’s pilot served as an airborne “quarterback” and gave high-level directives to an Anduril-made Fury CCA. The unmanned, semi-autonomous aircraft’s onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed the directives in real time, per the release, performing in-flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.
“This achievement demonstrates what is possible when we are aligned with industry on a shared imperative: delivering capability to the warfighter at unprecedented speed,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said in the announcement.
“We are driving urgency into every part of acquisition from rapid integration and flight learning to disciplined assessment, so we can turn promising technology into combat capability at the pace the threat demands,” he continued.
Personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group, Experimental Operations Unit, F-22 System Program Office and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch collaborated during the demonstration.
The service plans to use data from this event to inform software integration, developmental testing and further CCA concepts, the announcement says.
This test follows other milestones in the CCA development after the service announced its intention to have 500 combat-ready, semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet size of 1,000.
The Anduril-made Fury executed its first live-fire test by conducting an end-to-end, beyond-line-of-sight strike against a simulated target during a live-fire test at Edwards Air Force Base, California, in July.
Alongside Anduril’s CCA, the service has made strides with General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance, which was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nevada, last month to continue regular test and evaluation operations.
Anduril has yet to announce which Air Force base will house Fury, but Creech airmen conducted an Agile Combat Employment exercise earlier using the defense company’s aircraft, allowing airmen to complete sorties and build foundational tactics and procedures that will mold how CCA are integrated into the force.
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: Australia marks missile, cyber ‘firsts’ in exercise with Indonesia
articles.snippet: The Keris Woomera exercise comes during a busy month for Australia’s military, as forces participate in drills from Singapore to Japan.
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE — Australia and Indonesia have concluded a bilateral defense exercise that involved thousands of personnel and included a number of “firsts” for Canberra — the latest in what an analyst said were a series of trust-building and integration exercises between the nations.
Exercise Keris Woomera took place between October 12-20 in and around the eastern part of Indonesia’s most populous island of Java, and saw approximately 1,000 Australian personnel take part alongside their Indonesian counterparts. The Australian Department of Defence called Keris Woomera “the largest overseas training activity for the Australian Defence Force (ADF) for the year.”
“The exercise enables the Tentara Nasional Indonesia (TNI) to conduct high-end joint training with the ADF [Australian Defence Force], contributing to their own capacity to deter military coercion and defend Indonesian sovereignty,” the ADF said on its website.
It added that the exercise would “ensure ADF can deter a potential adversary’s attempts to project power against Australia, and be prepared to protect Australia and its maritime approaches.”
The ADF said the exercise played host to several firsts, including the “first time the high mobility artillery rocket system (HIMARS) deployed and fired overseas, the first deployment of an RAAF 4 Squadron aircraft into Southeast Asia since World War II and the first time Australia conducted cyber integration training with Indonesia.”
“By operating side-by-side, this year’s iteration has shown how Australia and Indonesia can integrate to address shared security challenges and positively impact how we respond to a rapidly evolving strategic environment.”
‘Increasingly Frequent Exercises’
The exercise comes just months after both countries signed the Australia-Indonesia Treaty on Common Security in February which, among other things, reaffirms the relationship between both countries and a desire “to contribute to regional security and stability”
Fauzan Malufti, a researcher at the Jakarta-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said that “Keris Woomera is part of a wider series of increasingly frequent exercises between the TNI and ADF, which will help build trust and familiarity at both the unit and leadership levels.”
He told Breaking Defense the exercise was expected to be confidence building for both sides and improve the interoperability.
“The exercise helps TNI and ADF better understand each other’s procedures, communications, planning and command systems so they can operate together better, especially in combat scenarios,” he added.
This year’s iteration of the exercise was the second in the series since the inaugural event in 2024, and Malufti said he believes that the Australians would like to see the exercise scale up in complexity as the regional security situation becomes more “challenging.”
He pointed out that Indonesia’s capabilities and other political considerations might nevertheless see it reluctant to widen the scope of future exercises, noting that Indonesia’s commitment to non-alignment might result in the nation not wanting to be seen as leaning towards any particular country.
“TNI capacity is another factor, as engagement with other foreign militaries is also increasing, while the TNI’s growing involvement in domestic non-defense activities continues to consume a huge number of resources and leadership attention”, he said.
Australia’s involvement in Keris Woomera comes amidst a busy October for its interactions with regional militaries. A detachment of its Lockheed Martin F-35 Lighting II fifth-generation fighters are currently deployed to Singapore as part of a contingent taking part in the Five Power Defence Arrangements exercise called Bersama Lima together with the militaries of Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore and the United Kingdom.
Another 300-strong contingent from the ADF is also currently in Japan participating in Exercise Keen Sword, where it is sending a frigate and a Boeing P-8A Poseidon multi-mission anti-submarine aircraft alongside the forces of Japan, the US and six other nations

articles.title: Pentagon weighs force posture, costs of rebuilding Middle East bases
articles.snippet: “We’re meeting with CENTCOM and doing the assessments right now from an installation perspective. Part of this is what will the global posture be in the future, and what does that require us to have?” a senior defense official told reporters today.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — As Pentagon leaders remain relatively tightlipped about the extent of damage to US bases in the Middle East, a senior US defense official said the administration is weighing possible force posture changes against costs as it decides which installations to rebuild.
“We’re meeting with CENTCOM [US Central Command] and doing the assessments right now from an installation perspective,” the senior defense official told reporters today at a Defense Writers Group breakfast. “Part of this is what will the global posture be in the future, and what does that require us to have?”
The official added that the department is taking a strategic approach to investments, prioritizing where its presence is needed most.
After the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, Tehran and its proxies began targeting US bases in the region — including Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, where strikes reportedly rendered the Pentagon’s Combined Air Operations Center (COAC) inoperable, as well as other installations in Saudi Arabia and Jordan.
The US Navy’s Fifth Fleet was previously headquartered at Naval Support Activity Bahrain. But in an interview with The Epoch Times, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao acknowledged that “they blew the hell out of Bahrain.” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle separately said the Navy would not be using Naval Support Activity Bahrain “anytime soon.”
Pentagon leaders have provided lawmakers with cost estimates for the war with Iran, but those figures have not included a complete account of the costs associated with repairing US bases in the region. Earlier this week, members of the Senate Armed Services Committee called on the department to publicly disclose the total cost of the war in Iran, including damage to those US installations.
The senior defense official said they did not have a cost estimate readily available but that the department was taking a strategic approach to repairs, noting that the changing threat environment means the Pentagon must rethink how it builds and protects its bases.
The proliferation of drones and cruise missiles presents another challenge, forcing the Pentagon to consider not only how to harden bases overseas but also how to protect installations on the US mainland, including through a diverse array of defense systems.
“The idea that we still have two oceans that keep any bad things from happening to us, that’s no longer a thing, so we’ve got to think differently. … The installation is the weapon system, and I have to have a mindset that I treat it like it’s a weapon system, not just a piece of real estate,” the official later added.
The official said the department is developing new approaches to making bases more resilient and defensible, protecting personnel and investing in a range of defensive measures rather than relying solely on physical fortifications.
Part of that effort involves strengthening protection at individual bases, as well as working with the Golden Dome team to prioritize which locations to protect first and keep “risk as low as possible,” they said.

articles.title: Norway to receive Chunmoos in 2028, reach IOC in 2029: Norwegian army leader
articles.snippet: Another component in deterring Russia, Acting Chief of the Norwegian Army Trond Nilsen told Breaking Defense, is having the Finnmark Brigade fully operational by 2032-2033.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Norway is set to begin receiving its 16 South Korean-made Chunmoo rocket artillery systems in 2028, the acting chief of the Norwegian army told Breaking Defense, as the country faces an increasing Russian threat.
“Initial capability is expected by 2029 and the operators will be trained in Norway. … The big advantage is that this [Chunmoo] will provide us with the ability to strike the enemy at long range,” Trond Nilsen told Breaking Defense during an interview on the sidelines of AUSA. According to promotional material, the Chunmoo has a range of approximately 500 kilometers (310.7 miles).
The Scandinavian country announced in January the procurement of the Chunmoo rocket artillery systems — a purchase valued at $2 billion by manufacturer Hanwha — as part of its long-range Arctic missile program.
The systems will be based in Bardufoss, in northern Norway. Following the January announcement of the contract, a report from the Independent Barents Observer quoted Norwegian Minister of Defense Tore O. Sandvik as stating that its missiles “might have sufficient range to hit the Pechenga Valley, where two of Russia’s most potent land forces are based: the 71st Guards Motorized Rifle Division and the 61st Naval Infantry Brigade,” highlighting the purchase’s strategic significance.
Another core component of Oslo’s response to deter Moscow, including along its 195-kilometer border with Russia, is the newly formed Finnmark Brigade, Nilsen explained.
“The reason we are building the Finnmark Brigade is the Russian threat; it is our response to that threat,” Nilsen said.
The unit, which was formally established in August 2025, was created to defend and patrol the country’s short but strategic border with Russia and is stationed in the far northern Arctic region. (Finnmark is located in the northeast corner of Norway, just above Finland and bordering Russia.)
Nilsen added that while the initial ambition was to equip the brigade with approximately 4,000 personnel and have it be fully operational by 2036, the timeline has been accelerated to now trying to accomplish this by 2032-2033.
“I am happy with how it is going, and according to plan, we are doing this as fast as possible,” the official said. He added that one of the main challenges has been building the infrastructure and accommodation needed to host that amount of forces and equipment.
Inspired by the success of drones in Ukraine against Russia, the Norwegian Army has also been rolling out a drone swarm pilot project involving intelligence-gathering and autonomous drones, Nilsen told Breaking Defense, with a goal of eventually fielding it to the Finnmark Brigade.
“The first thing we did was to launch drone strategies within the land forces and have some units develop their own — now almost all units in the army have some kind of drones,” Nilsen said.
While land forces are still testing the drones, Nilsen said, the plan is to begin using them in some operational units of the Finnmark Brigade within about a year.

articles.title: Northrop sees growing commercial market for microelectronics products
articles.snippet: “We could continue to solely invest in it ourselves with the support of our current shareholders. We could think about broadening that base of investments, or we could think … about separating the business,” Northrop CEO Kathy Warden said.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Northrop Grumman is bullish on expanding its microelectronics business to commercial customers, with the company undergoing a review of the business that could lead to a future spinoff or Pentagon investment, its chief executive said today.
In the company’s first major public statement since losing the Navy’s F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter competition, Northrop CEO Kathy Warden hinted that major changes to the company’s microelectronics unit are being considered.
“For more than a decade, we’ve leveraged our expertise in cutting-edge semiconductors and our secure US boundaries to pioneer leading quantum computing technologies,” Warden told investors during an earnings call this morning. “Today, we see a significant opportunity to scale this transformative technology for commercial and government customers.
“To fully realize its potential, we are actively evaluating strategic alternatives and believe we are uniquely positioned to lead in this field,” she said, adding that the company intends to share more details “in the coming months.”
Asked by analysts whether those changes included a sell-off or spin-off of the microelectronics business, Warden acknowledged that those two options are among those being considered, but that no final decisions have been made.
“We could continue to solely invest in it ourselves with the support of our current shareholders. We could think about broadening that base of investments, or we could think, as you noted, about separating the business,” Warden said.
“All of those options are on the table, and certainly the degree to which we do that and the timing are all the things that we would be taking under advisement here in the coming months,” she said.
The Army’s Digital Transformation
AI is reshaping the Army’s approach to cyber, electronic warfare and command and control. At TechNet Augusta 2026, leaders outlined how they’re turning emerging technology into capabilities for the battlefield.
Warden also did not preclude a direct investment from the Pentagon as an option. The department has announced a $1 billion equity stake in L3Harris’s missile solutions spin off, although that split has been postponed until mid-2027.
“We believe there is such a strong commercial application for this that we are not wanting to be overly dependent on any government, particularly the US government in this case. But all options are on the table,” Warden said.
The company’s microelectronics business — known as the Northrop Grumman Microelectronics Center — is made up of three government-accredited production facilities: two semiconductor foundries in California and Maryland and an advanced packaging facility in Florida.
While the majority of the company’s current work on microelectronics is geared toward the US government, Warden said those customers are “very open” to Northrop selling some of those products on the commercial market — which would also allow the company to sell those items to the government as commercial items.
“It’s an opportunity that, as a company, we are going to take advantage of in complete partnership with the government, but do it in a way that also opens up access to commercial markets that before we did not have as strong as an opportunity to pursue because of the restricted nature of the work we were doing,” she said.
One new technology that Warden said could have commercial applications is the Fortitude chip, which Northrop unveiled earlier this month. A gallium nitride chip the size of a grain of rice, Fortitude is designed to deliver three times more power and 20 times better signal quality as current chips, with applications including radar, GPs and future 6G networks, she said.
While most of the company’s current work in the sector centers on government customers, in previous decades, advances in microelectronics technology pioneered by Northrop have been harnessed in commercial technologies. One such example are the microchips used in cell phones during the early 2000s, according to the company.
Last fall, Northrop announced that it was now open to selling dozens of microelectronics components, made in government-certified facilities on US soil, to other aerospace and defense companies as a merchant supplier — a break from its previous position of manufacturing them only for Northrop-made products.
